questions.title: "Block‐diagonal versus full‐dense" — how do these two choices affect Orthogonal Finetuning?
questions.question_body: "I understand that Orthogonal Finetuning learns an orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf R\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) and applies it leftward to a frozen pretrained weight \(\mathbf W^0\). Instead of learning a full \(\mathbf R\), the authors sometimes replace \(\mathbf R\) by a block‐diagonal matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf R_1, … , \mathbf R_r)\), where every \(\mathbf R_i\in\mathbb R^{b \times b}\) has \(br=d\). What tradeoff emerges between having fewer trainable parameters (order \(bd\)) versus possessing fewer expressive degrees (only exploiting independent transformations on disjoint subspaces)? Could you give a concrete illustration showing situations where pairwise angles between neurons would fail to propagate across different blocks?

questions.title: "What exactly is meant by an information‑transmission graph over sparse matrices?
questions.question_body:
"The paper turns the factorisation \(\mathbf R = \mathbf B_m \cdots \mathbf B_1\) into a directed layered graph whose vertices are "nodes" at level \(j\in[1,m+1]\). An edge represents a non‑zero entry connecting two consecutive levels.

• How precisely do you construct this graph from a specific sparse matrix \(\mathbf B_i\)?
• What constraints derived from an orthogonality requirement translate into requirements on which edges must exist?
• When I read "every node in the first level should be able to reach every node in the last level" it feels reminiscent of connectivity theory – could you write down an exact combinatorial condition relating sparsity patterns so that their product becomes dense?

questions.title: "Why choose the Cayley transform for enforcing short‑term orthogonality?
questions.question_body:
"The authors parametrise "skew‑symmetric" matrices \(\mathbf Q=-\mathbf Q^{\top}\) via its Cayley transform \(\mathbf R=(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}\).

• Which properties make this representation preferable over alternatives such as antisymmetric exponential maps or Householder reflections?
• In particular, why does setting ‖Q‖₂≈0 initialise truly at identity while guaranteeing unitary evolution during stochastic optimisation?
• Are there known numerical stability concerns when ‖Q‖₂ approaches ½?

with vectors $d_i∈ℝ^{k/2}$. Vertically concatenating these produces a $d×k$ submatrix which itself lies inside increasingly larger square blocks until reaching full size $d$.

• Could you walk through an explicit example for $d=8$, listing back‑to‐back matrices “tilde B”(8,k)

questions.title: "How does multiplicative dropout work under winged beauty?
questions.question_body:
"Standard dropout zeros out individual elements additively drawn before applying linear layers.

In BOFT, authors describe picking percentages ‑ say p₁ parts out of *m* butterfly components ‑ then randomly turning p₂ fraction of diagonal blocks inside those selected components into identities.

• Concretely what operation replaces omitted submatrices?
• When you zero those submatrices effectively you still preserve global unitary property for remaining factors – is that guaranteed?
• And finally how hyperparameters p₁,p₂ relate empirically to over‑fitting prevention compared with LoRA’s elementwise mask?
